extracted.intended_audience: NLP/ML researchers, dataset users, authors and reviewers interested in computational analysis of peer review and building models using peer-review data
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and aspect-by-aspect scoring rubric used by ACL-style conference reviewers (and applied/annotated by the paper's authors) to evaluate submissions, plus procedural labeling rules for arXiv acceptance and operational signals correlated with acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness (1-5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the paper fit in ACL 2016? (Please answer this question in light of the desire to broaden the scope of the research areas represented at ACL.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 5: Certainly. 4: Probably. 3: Unsure. 2: Probably not. 1: Certainly not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity (1-5)
rubrics_metrics.description: For the reasonably well-prepared reader, is it clear what was done and why? Is the paper well-written and well-structured?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 5 = Very clear. 4 = Understandable by most readers. 3 = Mostly understandable to me with some effort. 2 = Important questions were hard to resolve even with effort. 1 = Much of the paper is confusing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality (1-5)
rubrics_metrics.description: How original is the approach? Does this paper break new ground in topic, methodology, or content? How exciting and innovative is the research it describes? Note that a paper could score high for originality even if the results do not show a convincing benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 5 = Surprising: Significant new problem, technique, methodology, or insight -- no prior research has attempted something similar. 4 = Creative: An intriguing problem, technique, or approach that is substantially different from previous research. 3 = Respectable: A nice research contribution that represents a notable extension of prior approaches or methodologies. 2 = Pedestrian: Obvious, or a minor improvement on familiar techniques. 1 = Significant portions have actually been done before or done better.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical Soundness / Correctness (1-5)
rubrics_metrics.description: First, is the technical approach sound and well-chosen? Second, can one trust the empirical claims of the paper -- are they supported by proper experiments and are the results of the experiments correctly interpreted?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 5 = The approach is very apt, and the claims are convincingly supported. 4 = Generally solid work, although there are some aspects of the approach or evaluation I am not sure about. 3 = Fairly reasonable work. The approach is not bad, and at least the main claims are probably correct, but I am not entirely ready to accept them (based on the material in the paper). 2 = Troublesome. There are some ideas worth salvaging here, but the work should really have been done or evaluated differently. 1 = Fatally flawed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theoretical Soundness / Correctness (1-5)
rubrics_metrics.description: First, is the mathematical approach sound and well-chosen? Second, are the arguments in the paper cogent and well-supported?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 5 = The mathematical approach is very apt, and the claims are convincingly supported. 4 = Generally solid work, although there are some aspects of the approach I am not sure about or the argument could be stronger. 3 = Fairly reasonable work. The approach is not bad, and at least the main claims are probably correct, but I am not entirely ready to accept them (based on the material in the paper). 2 = Troublesome. There are some ideas worth salvaging here, but the work should really have been done or argued differently. 1 = Fatally flawed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaningful Comparison (1-5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do the authors make clear where the problems and methods sit with respect to existing literature? Are the references adequate? For empirical papers, are the experimental results meaningfully compared with the best prior approaches?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 5 = Precise and complete comparison with related work. Good job given the space constraints. 4 = Mostly solid bibliography and comparison, but there are some references missing. 3 = Bibliography and comparison are somewhat helpful, but it could be hard for a reader to determine exactly how this work relates to previous work. 2 = Only partial awareness and understanding of related work, or a flawed empirical comparison. 1 = Little awareness of related work, or lacks necessary empirical comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substance (1-5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Does this paper have enough substance, or would it benefit from more ideas or results? (This question mainly concerns the amount of work; its quality is evaluated in other categories.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 5 = Contains more ideas or results than most publications in this conference; goes the extra mile. 4 = Represents an appropriate amount of work for a publication in this conference. (most submissions) 3 = Leaves open one or two natural questions that should have been pursued within the paper. 2 = Work in progress. There are enough good ideas, but perhaps not enough in terms of outcome. 1 = Seems thin. Not enough ideas here for a full-length paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact of Ideas or Results (1-5)
rubrics_metrics.description: How significant is the work described? If the ideas are novel, will they also be useful or inspirational? Does the paper bring any new insights into the nature of the problem?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 5 = Will affect the field by altering other people's choice of research topics or basic approach. 4 = Some of the ideas or results will substantially help other people's ongoing research. 3 = Interesting but not too influential. The work will be cited, but mainly for comparison or as a source of minor contributions. 2 = Marginally interesting. May or may not be cited. 1 = Will have no impact on the field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact of Accompanying Software (1-5)
rubrics_metrics.description: If software was submitted or released along with the paper, what is the expected impact of the software package? Will this software be valuable to others? Does it fill an unmet need? Is it at least sufficient to replicate or better understand the research in the paper?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 5 = Enabling: The newly released software should affect other people's choice of research or development projects to undertake. 4 = Useful: I would recommend the new software to other researchers or developers for their ongoing work. 3 = Potentially useful: Someone might find the new software useful for their work. 2 = Documentary: The new software useful to study or replicate the reported research, although for other purposes they may have limited interest or limited usability. (Still a positive rating) 1 = No usable software released.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact of Accompanying Dataset (1-5)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a dataset was submitted or released along with the paper, what is the expected impact of the dataset? Will this dataset be valuable to others in the form in which it is released? Does it fill an unmet need?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 5 = Enabling: The newly released datasets should affect other people's choice of research or development projects to undertake. 4 = Useful: I would recommend the new datasets to other researchers or developers for their ongoing work. 3 = Potentially useful: Someone might find the new datasets useful for their work. 2 = Documentary: The new datasets are useful to study or replicate the reported research, although for other purposes they may have limited interest or limited usability. (Still a positive rating) 1 = No usable datasets submitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation / Accept or Reject (1-5)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are many good submissions competing for slots at ACL 2016; how important is it to feature this one? Will people learn a lot by reading this paper or seeing it presented? Should the paper be accepted or rejected?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider all scores above when deciding. 5 = This paper changed my thinking on this topic and I'd fight to get it accepted. 4 = I learned a lot from this paper and would like to see it accepted. 3 = Borderline: I'm ambivalent about this one. 2 = Leaning against: I'd rather not see it in the conference. 1 = Poor: I'd fight to have it rejected. (Guidance also: remember authors have weeks to address reviewer comments; if a paper has weaknesses but is valuable, feel free to fight for it; convey ambivalence if you could live without it.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer Confidence (1-5)
rubrics_metrics.description: How confident is the reviewer that their evaluation is correct?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 5 = Positive that my evaluation is correct. I read the paper very carefully and am familiar with related work. 4 = Quite sure. I tried to check the important points carefully. It's unlikely, though conceivable, that I missed something that should affect my ratings. 3 = Pretty sure, but there's a chance I missed something. Although I have a good feel for this area in general, I did not carefully check the paper's details, e.g., the math, experimental design, or novelty. 2 = Willing to defend my evaluation, but it is fairly likely that I missed some details, didn't understand some central points, or can't be sure about the novelty of the work. 1 = Not my area, or paper is very hard to understand. My evaluation is just an educated guess.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aspect Scoring / Annotation Protocol (annotation of review text to aspect scores)
rubrics_metrics.description: Annotation protocol used by the paper authors to assign numeric aspect scores (1-5) based on review text for aspects: appropriateness, clarity, originality, soundness/correctness, meaningful comparison, substance, and impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Annotators read the review text (no access to the paper) and selected integer scores between 1–5 for each aspect; when review comments do not address a specific aspect, annotators mark it as 'not discussed' (special value). Feasibility: annotators inferred about half of the aspect scores from text. Agreement: on a sample of 30 reviews, 77% of annotations were consistent (exact or ±1), 2% were inconsistent (±2 or more); in 21% an aspect was 'not discussed' in one annotation but not the other. Annotators were provided the ACL 2016 instructions for each aspect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation-Format Recommendation Guidance (oral vs poster)
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance (from program chairs) for recommending whether an accepted submission should be an oral presentation or a poster.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Program chairs recommend reviewers and area chairs make this decision based on the expected size of interested audience and whether the ideas can be grasped without back-and-forth discussion. Empirical observation in PeerRead: reviews recommending oral presentation had higher mean overall recommendation (~0.9 higher) and higher mean substance and clarity scores; soundness/correctness may not align with oral recommendation.

rubrics_metrics.name: arXiv Accepted / Probably-Rejected Labeling Rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedural rules used to label arXiv submissions as 'accepted' or 'probably-rejected' with respect to a set of target top-tier venues (ACL, EMNLP, NAACL, EACL, TACL, NIPS, ICML, ICLR, AAAI).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accepted labeling: use Sutton and Gong (2017) DBLP-title/author matching; additionally add arXiv submission if its title matches an accepted paper with relative Levenshtein distance < 0.1. Probably-rejected labeling criteria (all required): (1) paper wasn't accepted to any target venues; (2) paper in arXiv categories cs.cl, cs.lg, or cs.ai; (3) not cross-listed in non-cs categories; (4) submission date within one month of submission deadlines of target venues (before or after); (5) submission date coincides with at least one of the arXiv papers accepted for one of the target venues. Data quality checks: search for author comments indicating acceptance; estimated small false negative rate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational Acceptance Signals / Features correlated with acceptance
rubrics_metrics.description: Features the authors used in their acceptance-classification models and features found to be salient in ablation studies (coarse and lexical features extracted from paper and metadata).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coarse features include: whether abstract contains keywords (deep, neural, embedding, outperform, novel, state_of_the_art), title_length, num_authors, most_recent_refs_year, num_refs, num_refmentions, avg_length_refs_mention, num_recent_refs, counts of figures/tables/sections/equations/theorems, num_uniq_words, num_sections, avg_sentence_length, contains_appendix, proportion of frequent words, bag-of-words/TFIDF of abstract, GloVe-based features. Ablation results (most salient features): appendix (removing decreased accuracy by up to 5.4% in ICLR), number of theorems, number of equations, avg_len_ref, presence of abstract phrase 'state_of_the_art' (ICLR) or 'neural' (arXiv), number of recent references, title length, num_uniq_words, num_refmentions. The authors note these features may correlate with strong papers or reviewer bias; models used hand-engineered features and standard classifiers.
